Relate the free energy change to the equilibrium constant:
ΔG° = −2.303 RT log K
Here ΔG° = −350 kJ, a large **negative** value. Rearranging:
log K = −ΔG°/(2.303RT) = +350000/(2.303RT)
The right-hand side is positive, so log K > 0 and therefore **K > 1** ✓
That makes (1) true: at equilibrium the products are favoured over the reactants.
(3) is false — a negative ΔG° means the reaction *is* thermodynamically feasible; that is
precisely what the sign tells you.
(4) is false — thermodynamics says nothing about speed. A reaction can have a large negative
ΔG° and still be immeasurably slow if its activation energy is high; diamond turning to
graphite is the standard example.
(2) cannot be decided from ΔG° alone, since ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° involves both terms.
∴ the equilibrium constant is greater than one.

kcet|Chemistry|2010|8||0|0.s:
A is p-nitrophenol and B is o-nitrophenol.
In **o**-nitrophenol the –OH and –NO₂ sit on adjacent carbons, close enough for the hydroxyl
hydrogen to bond to a nitro oxygen within the same molecule. That closes a six-membered ring:
intramolecular hydrogen bonding, or chelation.
Because the OH is already engaged internally, it cannot bond to neighbouring molecules.
In **p**-nitrophenol the two groups are at opposite ends, far too far apart for that, so each OH
bonds to the next molecule instead — intermolecular association, which effectively ties the
molecules together in larger units.
More intermolecular attraction means more energy needed to escape into the vapour, so A has
the lower vapour pressure and B the higher.
The same cause explains their melting points, 45 °C for the ortho isomer against 114 °C for
the para, and why the ortho isomer can be separated by steam distillation.
∴ higher than that of (A).

kcet|Chemistry|2010|9||0|0.s:
This is a strong acid with a strong base, so the heat released is the standard enthalpy of
neutralisation, 57.3 kJ per mole of water formed.
Find which reagent is limiting.
moles of HCl = 0.500 L × 0.1 mol L⁻¹ = 0.05 mol
moles of NaOH = 0.200 L × 0.2 mol L⁻¹ = 0.04 mol
NaOH is the smaller, so it is the limiting reagent and only 0.04 mol of water can form.
Heat evolved = 0.04 × 57.3 = 2.292 kJ
Using the HCl figure instead would give 0.05 × 57.3 = 2.865 kJ, which is not offered — a sign
that identifying the limiting reagent is the point of the question.
The value 57.3 kJ mol⁻¹ is the same for every strong acid–strong base pair, because the only
reaction actually occurring is H⁺ + OH⁻ ⇒ H₂O.
∴ 2.292 kJ.

kcet|Chemistry|2010|10||0|0:
Krypton on charcoal at low temperature is **physical** adsorption, held by van der Waals forces.
ΔS < 0 — the gas molecules lose their freedom to move in three dimensions and become
confined to the charcoal surface. Disorder falls, so entropy decreases.
ΔH < 0 — adsorption is exothermic. This follows necessarily: adsorption happens
spontaneously, so ΔG < 0, and with ΔS negative the term −TΔS is positive. For ΔG to come
out negative in spite of that, ΔH must be negative.
So both are negative, and the enthalpy term is what drives the process.
It also explains the phrase 'at low temperature' in the question: as T rises the positive −TΔS
term grows until it outweighs ΔH, ΔG turns positive and the krypton desorbs. That is why
physisorption always falls off with heating.
∴ ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0.

kcet|Chemistry|2010|11||0|0.s:
Copper is one of the irregular configurations: a filled 3d subshell is more stable than the
expected 3d⁹4s², so one 4s electron is promoted.
Cu (Z = 29) = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹
The **outermost** electron is the lone 4s electron — outermost means the highest principal
quantum number, n = 4, not the highest-energy subshell.
Now read off its four quantum numbers:
n = 4 (the fourth shell)
l = 0 (an s orbital)
m = 0 (an s orbital has only one orientation, so m can only be 0)
s = +½ (by convention for a single unpaired electron)
Options (1) and (3) describe d electrons (l = 2) and (2) a p electron (l = 1); all three are in
filled inner subshells, not the outermost.
∴ 4, 0, 0, +½.

kcet|Chemistry|2010|12||0|0.s:
The peroxide ion is O₂²⁻, with 16 + 2 = **18 electrons**. Fill the molecular orbitals:
σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s² σ*2s² σ2pz² π2px² π2py² π*2px² π*2py²
Now test each statement.
a) Diamagnetic ✓ — every orbital is doubly occupied, so there are no unpaired electrons. This
is the key difference from O₂ itself, which has two unpaired electrons in its π* orbitals.
d) Bond order one ✓ — bond order = (bonding − antibonding)/2 = (10 − 8)/2 = 1. That single
bond is why peroxides have a long, weak O–O link, 148 pm, and decompose so readily.
b) False — only **four** antibonding orbitals are filled: σ*1s, σ*2s, π*2px and π*2py. The
σ*2pz remains empty.
c) False — O₂²⁻ has 18 electrons, so it is isoelectronic with F₂, not with neon's 10. (A single
O²⁻ ion would be isoelectronic with neon, but the peroxide ion is diatomic.)
∴ only a) and d) are correct.

kcet|Chemistry|2010|13||0|0.s:
Find the statement that is not true.
(2) True — only one monosubstituted product forms, which is itself the evidence that all six
carbons are equivalent.
(3) True — the ring is planar with sp² carbons, so the angles are 120°.
(1) False — benzene does **not** contain three distinct single bonds and three distinct double
bonds. All six carbon–carbon bonds are identical, each 139 pm, lying between a single bond
(154 pm) and a double bond (134 pm), with a bond order of 1.5.
The six π electrons are not localised in three places; they are delocalised in rings above and
below the plane of the molecule.
That delocalisation is why benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition, and why its
heat of hydrogenation falls about 150 kJ mol⁻¹ short of the value predicted for three isolated
double bonds.
The Kekulé structure with alternating bonds is only a convenient drawing, not the real thing.
∴ statement (1) is not true.

kcet|Chemistry|2010|16||0|0:
Ionisation energy rises across a period, but dips whenever a stable filled or half-filled
subshell has to be broken into.
Check each pair, values in kJ mol⁻¹:
(3) Be 899 > B 801 — an **exception**. Beryllium has a filled 2s², while boron's electron comes
out of the higher-energy 2p.
(2) N 1402 > O 1314 — an **exception**. Nitrogen has a half-filled 2p³, and oxygen's fourth p
electron has to pair, bringing repulsion that makes it easier to remove.
(4) Mg 738 > Al 578 — an **exception**, the same filled-s against p case one period down.
(1) Na 496 < Mg 738 — this **increases**, exactly as the general trend predicts. Both are
filling the same 3s subshell, and magnesium simply has one more proton pulling on it.
So sodium and magnesium is the normal pair.
∴ Na and Mg is NOT an exception.

kcet|Chemistry|2010|17||0|0.s:
Work in milliequivalents throughout, since everything is given as normality.
meq = volume (cm³) × normality
Acid to be neutralised:
meq of HCl = 50 × 0.2 = 10
First part of the titration:
meq of NaOH added = 50 × 0.1 = 5
So the acid still unneutralised is
10 − 5 = 5 meq
That remainder is finished with 0.5 N KOH:
volume = meq / normality = 5 / 0.5 = 10 cm³
The point of using normality rather than molarity is that one milliequivalent of any base
neutralises exactly one milliequivalent of any acid, so NaOH and KOH can be added together
without worrying about their different formula masses.
∴ 10 cm³.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|1||0|0:
Froth flotation is the method for **sulphide** ores. A collector such as potassium ethyl
xanthate makes the sulphide surface water repellent, so the ore particles cling to the air
bubbles and rise with the froth, while the wetted gangue sinks.
Check each ore:
(4) Cinnabar, HgS — a sulphide ✓ concentrated by froth flotation
(1) Bauxite, Al₂O₃·2H₂O — an oxide, purified by the Bayer leaching process
(2) Malachite, CuCO₃·Cu(OH)₂ — a carbonate
(3) Zincite, ZnO — an oxide
Oxide and carbonate surfaces are polar and are wetted by water, so they cannot be floated;
they are concentrated by gravity separation, magnetic separation or leaching instead.
The rule is worth remembering as a pair: froth flotation for sulphides, and sulphides are then
roasted, while carbonates are calcined.
∴ cinnabar.
